strengths: The work addresses an important and comparatively underexplored problem: spatial reasoning across multiple views. MultiSPA is substantial in scale (over 27M QA pairs from 1.1M images) and covers 26 subtasks with varied references and outputs, including coordinates, metric values, and 3D vectors.

The data-generation pipeline uses calibrated geometry, depth, camera poses, and tracked 3D points rather than relying primarily on noisy model-generated spatial labels. Scene-disjoint evaluation splits, overlap-balanced view sampling, and motion-balanced sampling are sensible design choices.

The main results are strong and consistent across the proposed benchmark: fine-tuning InternVL2-8B raises average accuracy from 20.43% to 56.11%, with improvements on every reported category. Difficult quantitative tasks remain far from solved, so the results do not merely reflect saturation of easy questions.

External evaluation provides meaningful evidence beyond the authors' generated benchmark. On the relevant BLINK subsets, the model improves the InternVL2-8B average from 57.9% to 84.3%, including a large multi-view reasoning gain from 49.6% to 94.7%. Standard VQA performance is also largely retained.

The scaling and multi-task comparisons are useful: camera-vector accuracy increases with both data and model size, while adding other spatial tasks improves camera-vector accuracy from 9.3% to 18.0% and object-motion accuracy from 17.5% to 22.04%. These experiments support the practical value of the dataset and joint training.
weaknesses: The principal benchmark is generated by the same pipeline, source datasets, task definitions, and apparently closely related templates used for training. Holding out scenes prevents direct image leakage but does not test robustness to new annotation conventions or question formulations. Image/frame-shuffling controls, held-out template families, or additional external metric-spatial benchmarks would be needed to rule out dataset-specific shortcuts more convincingly.

The automatic dataset receives no quantitative quality audit. In particular, projected visibility and correspondence labels, motion labels, rigid-body clustering, and object dimensions can inherit reconstruction, depth, tracking, and bounding-box errors. The paper provides examples but no manual precision study, uncertainty filtering analysis, or sensitivity analysis for generation thresholds.

Evaluation details introduce avoidable ambiguity. Numerical predictions are converted to accuracy using relatively permissive thresholds, binary motion-direction labels appear to lack a dead zone for negligible motion, and results are reported without confidence intervals or multiple seeds. GPT-4 post-processing is applied to baseline outputs but not the trained model, and the prompts and post-processing behavior are insufficiently specified to establish complete fairness and reproducibility.

The claimed emergent behavior is not established. The experiment contains only three model configurations, changes vision-encoder and language-model capacity together, uses one task and apparently one run, and shows degradation for the two smaller models followed by a jump for the largest. This is compatible with an optimization or capacity threshold but is insufficient evidence for emergence.

Most experiments use only two frames, as acknowledged by the authors, despite the broader multi-frame framing. The robotics evidence is also only a small qualitative demonstration; it does not validate the proposed use as a reliable reward annotator.

The comparison suite is narrow for a CVPR 2026 claim: open-model comparisons are confined to the InternVL2 family, and the directly related SAT approach is discussed but not evaluated. Important reproducibility information is also missing or deferred, including the exact 3M-sample composition, full templates, sampling parameters, random seeds, and complete release details. These are meaningful limitations, but they do not outweigh the supported dataset and modeling contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: training MLLMs for metric and qualitative spatial reasoning across views rather than only within one image.

MultiSPA is substantial in scale and scope, with 27M generated QA samples, 1.1M images, 26 subtasks, multiple reference types, and outputs ranging from labels to coordinates and 3D vectors. Its geometry-based generation from depth, camera poses, and tracked points is preferable to relying entirely on noisy pseudo-labels.

The reported improvements are large and consistent across the internal benchmark. More importantly, the external BLINK evaluation provides some evidence of transfer: the model improves from 57.9 to 84.3 average over its InternVL-8B base and reaches 94.7 on Multi-View Reasoning.
Standard VQA results remain reasonably close to the base model, suggesting that specialization does not catastrophically erase general capabilities.
The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and unusually explicit about task definitions, answer formats, training resources, and several data-generation algorithms.
weaknesses: The primary evaluation is circular: training and testing use the same generation pipeline, source datasets, task definitions, answer tolerances, and apparently closely related templates, with only scenes or scenarios held out. The comparison against untuned base and proprietary models therefore demonstrates the benefit of in-distribution supervision more convincingly than general multi-frame spatial understanding.

Crucial controls are absent. There are no single-frame, image-order-shuffled, second-image-masked, correspondence-destroyed, or language/category-prior baselines. Consequently, the experiments do not establish how often the model genuinely integrates multiple views rather than exploiting monocular depth cues, object-size priors, dataset regularities, or template-specific associations. This is especially important because depth estimation is explicitly single-image and most remaining tasks use only two views.

The claimed multi-task synergy is confounded by training-set size: camera motion compares 500K single-task samples against 3M multi-task samples, while object motion compares 400K against 800K total samples. Equal-budget and additional-same-task controls are needed before attributing the gains to task diversity.

The evidence for emergence is inadequate. It consists of only three model configurations, changes both vision-encoder and language-model capacity, reports no repeated runs or uncertainty, and examines a single task. A jump at 26B under these confounds does not establish emergent behavior.

The benchmark uses only 300 examples per subtask, reports no confidence intervals or variation across training runs, and employs scale-dependent 20% error thresholds. The latter become extremely strict near zero and increasingly permissive for large motions. Direction labels also appear to be assigned solely by sign, without a dead zone for negligible or noisy motion.

Dataset quality is insufficiently validated. There is no manual audit, annotation-error estimate, per-source/task distribution, duplicate analysis, or systematic study of reconstruction and tracking noise. Only 3M of the advertised 27M samples are used for the principal model, leaving the quality and utility of most of the dataset unsupported.

Several details needed for reproduction remain ambiguous or omitted, including the exact computation and coordinate frame for object displacement under simultaneous camera motion, full template lists, task-mixture proportions, filtering thresholds, and benchmark post-processing. Using GPT-4 to normalize baseline answers may additionally introduce model-dependent evaluation effects without an ablation.

The robotics claim is supported only by one qualitative sequence. There is no task-level evaluation, reward correlation study, or robot-learning experiment, so the evidence supports an illustrative possibility rather than a demonstrated reward annotator.

Overall, the dataset and external BLINK result are worthwhile, but the missing shortcut controls, internally matched benchmark, and confounded headline analyses leave the central scientific claim insufficiently isolated for a clear acceptance recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: quantitative spatial understanding across multiple frames. The five task families cover complementary capabilities, including correspondence, depth, camera motion, object motion, and object size.

MultiSPA is a substantial resource: it contains more than 27M QA samples derived from 1.1M images, supports several reference and answer formats, and uses scene-disjoint training and evaluation splits. The geometry-based generation pipeline is more compelling than relying solely on noisy pseudo-labels from monocular estimators.

The main empirical gains are large and consistent. The 8B model improves the MultiSPA average from 20.43% to 56.11%, with particularly strong gains in depth value estimation, coordinate correspondence, and camera orientation. Its remaining low scores on vector prediction are reported candidly.

External evaluation provides meaningful evidence beyond the authors' benchmark. On the relevant BLINK subsets, the model reaches an 84.3% average versus 57.9% for its InternVL-8B base and 75.7% for the strongest reported proprietary baseline. Standard VQA results also suggest that spatial fine-tuning largely preserves general capabilities.

The paper is clear, visually polished, and unusually concrete about data construction, task definitions, coordinate conventions, optimization, compute, and limitations. weaknesses: The central benchmark comparison mainly contrasts a model trained on MultiSPA against general-purpose models that receive no comparable spatial supervision. This establishes the value of task-specific training, but does not isolate the benefit of the particular data engine or compare adequately with specialized multi-frame methods such as SAT. The model contribution itself is conventional LoRA fine-tuning rather than a new architecture.

The evidence for multi-task synergy is confounded by training volume. Camera-vector training compares 500K single-task examples against the full 3M multi-task set; the object-motion experiment compares 400K examples against 800K total examples. Neither comparison controls total sample count or contrasts auxiliary-task data with additional target-task data, so the results do not yet establish synergy rather than a generic benefit from more training.

The claimed emergent behavior is only weakly supported. It is inferred from one hard-to-easy correspondence experiment, without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, and the compared model sizes also change the vision encoder and language backbone. This result is interesting, but cannot distinguish emergence from architecture, optimization, or a smooth capacity threshold.

The robotics application is illustrative rather than validated: Figure 5 contains a small qualitative demonstration and does not evaluate reward quality, policy learning, task success, or robustness. Accordingly, the evidence supports potential use as a reward annotator, not demonstrated practical effectiveness.

Evaluation details leave some reproducibility and interpretation concerns. The 20%-relative-error rule is sensitive to ground-truth magnitude and is problematic near zero; the tolerance choices are not justified; GPT-4 post-processing of baseline outputs may affect fairness; and no confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are reported for 300-example subtask sets.

Only 3M of the advertised 27M QA samples are used for the principal model, but the exact per-task mixture and selection procedure are not fully specified. Complete templates are deferred to a project website, while release details for data, code, checkpoints, and proprietary-model post-processing prompts are not provided in the manuscript. These are meaningful reproducibility limitations, though they do not outweigh the demonstrated dataset and empirical contribution.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: metric spatial understanding across multiple images. MultiSPA is unusually large (27M QA pairs from 1.1M images) and covers a useful range of capabilities, reference types, and outputs, including depth, correspondence, camera/object motion, coordinates, and 3D vectors.

The data-generation framework makes effective use of geometric annotations from ScanNet and TAPVid3D-derived sources. Balanced sampling by overlap and motion magnitude, scene-disjoint evaluation splits, and rigid-part sampling are thoughtful design choices.

The main empirical gains are large and consistent across every MultiSPA category: the 8B model improves average accuracy from 20.43 to 56.11. Scaling and fine-tuning ablations further show that more data, model capacity, and vision-encoder tuning improve difficult quantitative tasks.

Evidence extends beyond the paper's own benchmark. Zero-shot BLINK performance rises from 57.9 to 84.3, with especially strong correspondence and multi-view gains; improvements are also reported on 3RScan, ERQA multi-view, and CVBench-3D.

Evaluation on ten conventional VQA benchmarks indicates that spatial fine-tuning largely preserves general capabilities. The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and candid that its data predominantly contain two-frame examples.
weaknesses: The strongest results use a benchmark generated by the same pipeline, source datasets, task definitions, answer templates, and annotation conventions as training. Although scenes are disjoint and external benchmarks help, this makes the 35.68-point headline gain partly a measure of in-distribution task-format adaptation. Broader quantitative evaluation on independently constructed metric-motion datasets is missing.

Important annotation and metric choices are insufficiently validated. The visibility test accepts every projected point in front of the depth map without a tolerance or reported annotation audit. Object 'width' and 'length' are taken from 3D bounding-box axes, but the paper does not establish that these axes consistently correspond to the semantic dimensions named in questions. No manual precision study is provided for the 27M generated samples.

The relative-error rule is problematic near zero: requiring ||prediction−GT|| <= 0.2||GT|| becomes extremely strict or exact for small/static motions, while direction labels are assigned purely from coordinate signs without a dead zone for negligible motion. Coordinate correctness is also described ambiguously as being within '5% image width pixels,' including for the vertical coordinate. Results are therefore difficult to interpret across motion scales.

The claimed multi-task 'synergy' is confounded by additional training data and optimization steps. For example, 500K camera-only samples are compared with 3M mixed samples, and 400K object-motion samples with versus without 400K extra samples. Sample-budget-matched same-task or control mixtures are needed to distinguish cross-task transfer from ordinary benefits of more supervision.

The 'emergent' behavior claim is based on only three model configurations, with changes in encoder size and possibly optimization behavior, and no repeated runs or uncertainty. A sharp improvement at one scale does not by itself distinguish emergence from a smooth but sparsely sampled scaling trend; this should be framed only as a preliminary observation.

Despite the multi-frame framing, almost all training uses image pairs. The more-frame experiment only inserts intermediate images while querying the first-to-last motion; unchanged performance could equally mean that the model ignores those intermediate frames, so it does not demonstrate integration of evidence from more than two views.

Comparisons with expert systems are not sufficiently controlled or documented: VGGT receives unspecified scale normalization, different fine-tuned model variants are used for different tasks, and the exact conversion of expert outputs to benchmark decisions is absent. Proprietary baselines additionally undergo GPT-4 post-processing without enough detail to rule out content changes.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of a stated code/data release, complete template set, exact 3M-sample mixture, LoRA target modules, preprocessing details, random seeds, and variability across runs. The robotics reward-annotation result is also only a single qualitative sequence and cannot support effectiveness in robot learning.

strengths: The paper tackles an important limitation of current MLLMs: spatial perception across multiple views. Organizing the problem around depth, correspondence, camera motion, object motion, and object size is useful for both research and embodied applications.

MultiSPA is a substantial contribution: it contains over 27M generated QA samples from 1.1M images, supports several reference/output formats, and is built from geometrically annotated real-world datasets rather than only simulation or noisy pseudo-labels.

The main empirical gains are large and consistent. On the authors' scene-disjoint MultiSPA benchmark, the 8B model improves the average from 20.43 to 56.11 and improves every reported subtask, including quantitative correspondence and motion outputs where baseline models are near zero.

There is meaningful evidence beyond the proposed benchmark. On the relevant BLINK subsets, the model improves over InternVL2-8B from 57.9 to 84.3, including a particularly large multi-view-reasoning gain from 49.6 to 94.7. Improvements are also reported on CVBench-3D and the multi-view subset of ERQA, and a separate 3RScan experiment tests camera-vector prediction on unseen synthetic renders.

The study includes useful scaling and adaptation analyses. Performance generally increases with training data, model capacity, and the number of trainable components; Table 8 in particular shows that tuning the visual encoder materially improves fine-grained spatial tasks.

General VQA evaluations suggest that spatial fine-tuning does not cause severe catastrophic forgetting. Although several individual scores decline slightly, performance remains broadly comparable across ten reported benchmarks.
The manuscript is generally clear and supplies training hyperparameters, dataset distributions, task templates, generation equations, and simplified implementations of important sampling procedures.
weaknesses: The primary benchmark is generated with the same source datasets, task definitions, answer templates, and annotation pipeline as the training data. Scene-disjoint splitting prevents direct image leakage, but the very large MultiSPA gains primarily demonstrate interpolation within this constructed task distribution. BLINK and the other external evaluations help substantially, but they cover only part of the proposed quantitative task set.

The claimed multi-task 'synergy' is not isolated from training volume or optimization budget. The camera experiment compares 500K single-task samples against 3M multi-task samples, while the object-motion experiment adds another 400K samples to a 400K baseline. The supplementary correspondence experiments similarly add data. These results establish that additional related supervision helps, but not that task diversity itself is responsible.

The evidence for emergent spatial understanding is inadequate. Table 6 contains only three configurations and simultaneously changes encoder size, language-model size, and total capacity. The 8B and 13B models becoming slightly worse while the 26B model improves could reflect architecture, optimization, or sample-efficiency differences rather than an emergent threshold. This claim should not be presented as a finding in the abstract and conclusion.

Several evaluation choices require stronger justification and sensitivity analysis. A scalar or vector is counted correct under a 20% relative-error threshold, coordinates use a 5%-of-image-width tolerance, and only 300 examples are evaluated per subtask. No uncertainty estimates or repeated runs are reported. In particular, relative error is ill-behaved for zero or near-zero motion, which is relevant to the stated static-object use case.

The comparison with specialist models is not fully controlled. VGGT is evaluated only after scale normalization even though MultiSPA emphasizes metric vectors; different tasks use different model variants and training regimes; and the reported comparison reduces each expert system to one thresholded accuracy. Thus the claim of matching specialized 3D models is weaker than the tables imply.

Baseline evaluation is insufficiently reproducible. Proprietary-model responses are post-processed by GPT-4, but the exact prompting, post-processing instructions, failure handling, and possible effect on answers are not documented. Full dataset templates, exact split lists, and production implementations are also absent; the appendix explicitly provides only partial templates and simplified code.

Annotation validity is not directly audited. There is no manual quality study or analysis of errors from camera poses, reconstructed geometry, visibility tests, and tracked points. Object dimensions are derived from 3D bounding boxes, but the paper does not clarify whether width and length are object-oriented or tied to dataset/world axes; the latter would make their semantic interpretation depend on object orientation.

The claimed robotic reward-annotation application is supported only by a small qualitative demonstration. Figure 5 shows that predicted distances follow an increasing trend but remain quantitatively inaccurate; it does not evaluate reward quality, policy learning, task success, or robustness. It should therefore be framed strictly as an illustrative possibility.

The treatment of more than two frames is limited. Nearly all training uses pairs, and the supplementary test merely inserts intermediate frames while asking for motion between the endpoints. Its nearly unchanged accuracy is compatible with ignoring the added frames, so it does not show that the model integrates information from longer sequences.

strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored problem: extending MLLM spatial understanding from individual images to multiple frames, including correspondence, camera motion, object motion, depth, and object size. The combination of tasks, reference types, and structured outputs is broader than most prior spatial-VLM datasets.

MultiSPA is a substantial contribution: the pipeline converts aligned 3D/4D annotations into more than 27M QA samples from 1.1M images, with scene-disjoint benchmark splits. Balanced sampling by overlap and motion magnitude and the rigid-part sampling strategy are sensible design choices. The central empirical result is convincing: the 8B model improves the MultiSPA average from 20.43 to 56.11, with large gains on quantitative tasks such as coordinate correspondence, metric depth, and camera-motion estimation. The improvement is consistent across all reported task groups rather than being driven by one benchmark.

Evidence of transfer strengthens the contribution. The model improves substantially on BLINK, particularly multi-view reasoning (49.6 to 94.7), and improves the multi-view ERQA subset (13.5 to 21.6). Results on ten general VQA benchmarks and the training-time forgetting curve indicate that the spatial fine-tuning largely preserves general capabilities.

The ablations cover data scale, model capacity, trainable components, task combinations, and external specialist systems. In particular, the large gains from tuning the vision encoder provide a useful practical finding, while comparisons with VGGT, Depth Anything, and LoFTR suggest that a general-purpose VLM can acquire meaningful geometric abilities.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, provides equations for data construction and evaluation, reports major optimization and compute settings, and includes representative examples and simplified algorithms in the appendix.
weaknesses: Material: the evidence for “multi-task synergy” is confounded by training-set size. For example, camera motion is compared using 500K single-task samples versus the full 3M set, and object motion uses 400K single-task samples versus 800K mixed samples. Tables 12–13 have similar unequal-data comparisons. These experiments show that additional related data helps, but do not establish synergy beyond ordinary scaling; equal-total-sample controls are needed for that claim.

Material: the “emergent” behavior claim is substantially stronger than the evidence. It rests on three model configurations, with model size entangled with vision-encoder size, apparently without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. The unusual hard-training/easy-testing protocol and the sharp 26B result are interesting observations, but insufficient to distinguish emergence from optimization, architecture, or capacity effects.

Material: most benchmark results are generated from the same source datasets and template pipeline as training, albeit with held-out scenes. There is no reported manual audit of label correctness, ambiguity, or template artifacts. External benchmarks partly address transfer, but the gains are uneven: spatial reasoning in BLINK declines slightly, CVBench-3D improves by only 3.5 points, and overall ERQA by 0.4 points.

Material: the numerical evaluation uses a single thresholded accuracy—20% relative error for scalar/vector outputs and 5% image width for coordinates—without continuous errors, threshold sensitivity, or uncertainty. Relative tolerance is especially problematic near zero, relevant because the object-motion data explicitly includes static points. Reporting median/mean geometric errors and performance by motion or depth range would make the quantitative claims more robust.

Material: the robotics reward-annotation application is only a qualitative example from one sequence. It shows promising out-of-domain behavior but does not substantiate usefulness as a reward model, since no task-level robot-learning outcome, calibration analysis, or broader sequence evaluation is reported.

The evaluation with more frames does not demonstrate that the model uses additional views: inserting intermediate frames leaves accuracy essentially unchanged while the question concerns only the first and last frames. This establishes robustness to extra inputs, not improved multi-view integration. Moreover, most training tasks use only two frames and even the minimum-coverage object-size procedure is capped at two.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful implementation details. The paper omits full generation templates, several sampling quotas and filtering thresholds, random seeds or variance across runs, and sufficiently detailed protocols for the specialist-model comparisons. The use of GPT-4 post-processing for baseline outputs also needs an audit showing that it preserves answer semantics and does not affect comparison fairness.

Presentation refinement: claims such as “first,” “comprehensive,” and matching specialized models should be qualified more carefully. The specialist comparisons use task-specific models, training configurations, and scale normalization, while the concurrent SAT work already studies multi-frame spatial reasoning. These issues temper the framing but do not negate the paper’s substantive dataset and empirical contribution.
